analysis.title: Democratic sweep: What changes for the US economy and financial markets?
key_insights: Democrats won both the House and Senate and a majority of governorships in the 4 November 2026 midterms. Results are not definitive, but the majorities are described as decisive. Near-term policy is little changed because Democrats lack a filibuster-proof Senate majority and President Trump retains veto power.

Fiscal policy is expected to deadlock, with rising risk of a government shutdown, a debt-ceiling standoff and wider deficits. Funding and debt-ceiling deadlines could converge in Q4 2027 to Q1 2028. Republicans may pass more defense funds or raise the debt ceiling before year-end.

Expected 2027 compromise: Republicans get about USD90bn in supplemental defense spending to replenish munitions, with about USD50bn paid out in 2027. Democrats get higher non-defense spending and delayed OBBB health and nutrition cuts. The fiscal stance is slightly loose at 0.2% of GDP. A re-escalation with Iran could delay the defense money.

The federal deficit is forecast to widen from -6.2% of GDP in 2026 to -6.6% in 2027 and -6.4% in 2028. The primary deficit goes from -2.8% to -3.0% of GDP in 2027. Interest expense rises from 3.6% to 3.8% of GDP.

Tariff, immigration and regulatory policy stay largely executive-led. The effective US tariff rate is expected to reach about 8.5% by January 2027 as new Section 301 tariffs are implemented. Effective rates are projected at 8-9% on the EU, 29% on China and 11% on Japan.
A Democratic Senate will mainly slow confirmations, including for the Fed vacancy when Powell's term ends in January 2028. This eases concerns over Fed independence.

Oil is the main link between the midterms and inflation. A brief resumption of fighting with Iran could push oil to about USD130/bbl, 15-20% above current levels. Congress cannot constrain military action before the new Congress convenes in January, and the President could veto funding restrictions.

A renewed Iran escalation would likely cause an oil-driven inflation shock, a bear flattening of the Treasury curve and a more hawkish Fed. Rates volatility and the term premium would rise. Over a longer horizon, weak growth could support long-dated Treasuries through safe-haven demand.

Risks for US equities are tilted to the downside. The S&P 500 has tracked past midterm years in which the president's party lost a chamber. Elevated yields limit multiple expansion. Tech is most exposed to state-level AI regulation and Iran. Initial reaction was modestly negative, with S&P 500 futures down 0.3% and Nasdaq futures down 0.4%, and Asian tech-heavy indices down 3-4%. The report does not expect strong corrections.

Sector view: healthcare is the best-placed defensive and energy is a hedge against Iran escalation. Technology (semis and AI infrastructure) is negative. Financials, industrials and defense, real estate and energy are neutral. Staples and restaurants are positive. Consumer discretionary is negative to neutral. Utilities are neutral to positive.

AI policy stays light-touch federally, but the fight moves to the states, which control permitting, siting and utility rates. Democrats won seven of ten competitive governor races covering 67 GW of planned data-center capacity, with three races uncalled. Governors-elect backing a full or conditional moratorium preside over about 47 GW (70%). OpenAI has 14.1 GW planned in these ten states, more than Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta combined.

Local opposition blocked or delayed nearly USD200bn of data-center projects in H1 2026. New York imposed the first statewide moratorium in July. 261 local moratoria are in force and 26 states are considering statewide ones. 79% of Americans favor AI regulation and 71% oppose a data center in their community (Allianz Pulse and Gallup).

AI-related investment accounts for more than a third of 2026 GDP growth. The four largest hyperscalers are expected to spend about USD725bn in capex in 2026, up 77% from USD410bn in 2025. Delays would weigh on growth and on tech valuations premised on capex growth.

US GDP is forecast to grow 2.4% in 2026, up from 2.1% in the September scenario. CPI is forecast above 4% by early 2027 and above 3% through October 2027. September CPI was 3.7% against 3.0% wage growth, so real wages are negative. Saving rate fell from 5.6% in January to 3.8% in September.

Housing: mortgage rates are up about 140bps year to date and the 30-year fixed is above 7%. Pending home sales hit a record low in September. Income needed to afford the median home is about USD121,000, up from USD111,000 in February. Housing policy may be an area of bipartisan compromise.

Credit followed the usual midterm pattern, weak into the vote. High yield excess return was -1.7% from August to October, worse than in five of the previous seven midterm cycles. Investment grade was -0.6%. Spreads are near cycle tights, and the direction after the vote depends on the Fed and on supply. The report cites a Fed expected to tighten further and a 10-year yield near 5%.

In the seven midterm years since the mid-1960s when the president's party lost a chamber, the S&P 500 was +4.3% at end-October and ended the year 6.7% above its 1 July level. In the eight years when the party kept control, it fell almost 5.5% in early October and ended 2.4% above its 1 July level.

Private markets: expect selectivity rather than retrenchment. Oversight hearings are likely to target private credit and PE in healthcare and housing. Sweeping tax changes to private markets are unlikely before 2028. Higher long-term rates of up to 30bps and a possible shutdown or debt-ceiling standoff keep financing costs elevated.

A Treasury market intervention may be needed if rates volatility stays high. Treasury would likely act first through expanded buybacks or changes to issuance mix. A Fed led by Kevin Warsh would probably stay reluctant to provide accommodation while inflation is above target.

sector_views.rationale: Partial relief on ACA subsidies and Medicaid is more likely. It is the best-placed defensive and the least rate-sensitive.
AI guardrails and data-center restrictions become more likely, and consensus earnings leave little room for disappointment.
A Democratic Senate could slow bank deregulation, but rules run through the agencies. Expect a headline dip, not a reversal.
Less deregulation, but still a hedge against Iran re-escalation. It is the sector most likely to outperform if Iran escalates.
More support for renewables, but rates cap the upside. The report calls it neutral to positive.
Stronger pressure to soften benefit cuts, while the veto limits what can pass.
Household pressure persists with limited help from softer benefit cuts. The report calls it negative to neutral.
The USD500bn defense hike is likely rejected, while a USD90bn supplemental is likely.
A 2018-style run needs lower yields, which is not the baseline.

earnings_insights: The report says the Q3 earnings season has been quite strong so far. No company-level EPS or revenue figures are given.
The report says consensus earnings leave little room for disappointment in tech. A renewed Iran escalation would hit margins through higher input costs and a pressured consumer.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Raised from +2.1% in the September scenario. AI-driven business investment supports growth.
Above wage growth of 3.0%, so real wages are negative.
The inflation shock is concentrated in energy rather than a wage-price spiral.

macro_indicators.reading: above +4% by early 2027, above +3% through October 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: Raised on geopolitical tension and energy prices.
Weakest pace since early 2020, consistent with a low-hire labor market.
Energy shock after the Iran war is feeding voter frustration.
Near historical lows, but job creation has stalled since last year.
Down from 5.6% in January. Households rely on savings, borrowing and wealth effects.
Up about 140bps since the start of the year, so housing affordability is under pressure.
Wider deficits as defense and non-defense spending rise and interest costs climb.

macro_indicators.reading: 0.2% of GDP loosening in 2027, 0.4% tightening in 2028
macro_indicators.interpretation: Compromise spending loosens policy in 2027 before tightening in 2028.
Reflects new Section 301 tariffs. It was over 7% estimated in September 2026.
Elevated yields limit scope for equity multiple expansion.

macro_indicators.indicator: Oil price in an Iran escalation
macro_indicators.interpretation: 15-20% above current levels. It would feed an inflation shock and a bear flattening of the Treasury curve.

crypto_views: The GENIUS Act created a federal stablecoin regime in 2025. The CLARITY market-structure bill stalled in the Senate in September.
A Democratic House is expected to hold hearings and subpoenas on cryptocurrency, with Maxine Waters returning as chair of the Financial Services Committee.

trade_ideas.description: Long-end versus front-end Treasury curve steepening-reversal: long-dated Treasuries outperform the front end if equities correct and recession risk takes over from inflation risk
trade_ideas.rationale: Weak real disposable income, slowing job creation and falling savings make the economy vulnerable to a demand shock that revives safe-haven demand for duration.
trade_ideas.risk: A structurally higher term premium would limit the move.

trade_ideas.description: Energy sector as a hedge against Iran re-escalation
trade_ideas.rationale: Energy is the sector most likely to outperform if Iran escalates again and offsets the risk weighing on other sectors.

risk_factors: Renewed military escalation with Iran leading to an oil spike and an inflation shock.
Government shutdown and debt-ceiling standoff converging in Q4 2027 to Q1 2028. The first funding test comes 11 December 2026.
Tariff escalation and institutional friction between the executive and legislative branches.
State-level AI regulation and data-center moratoria slowing the AI buildout.
Higher term premium and Treasury volatility from fiscal deterioration.
K-shaped consumption exposed to an AI-driven equity valuation correction.
Credit weakness, with record AI-related issuance and spreads near cycle tights.
charts_described: Figure 6 plots average S&P 500 performance around midterm years against other years and against years when the president's party wins or loses, indexed from July to December, with 2026 overlaid.
Figure 7 plots credit excess returns for investment grade and high yield in midterm versus non-midterm years from August to February.
Figure 1 plots US CPI inflation against average hourly earnings growth, y/y in %, with prices outpacing wages since April 2026.
vol_and_positioning: The report expects higher equity volatility, since a change of control adds index-level uncertainty.
Rates volatility is expected to stay elevated because of political uncertainty, weaker market liquidity and a hawkish Fed. Treasury-led intervention may be needed to preserve market functioning.
A renewed Iran shock would likely push the crude curve into steep backwardation.
geopolitical: A resumption of military action against Iran is the main upside risk to oil and wholesale gas prices. A Democratic Congress has limited ability to prevent it before January.
Possible tariff escalation with Canada, including 50% tariffs on Canadian motor vehicles, and threats to pull out of the USMCA.
Possible US retaliation against European countries over the Global Service Tax, and another wave of Section 301 tariffs on transshipped goods.
Data centers within Iran's reach could become targets if strikes resume, which would be a physical risk to the AI build-out.

tension_points.bull_case: Election outcomes rarely drive markets. In years when the president's party lost a chamber, the S&P 500 held up through autumn and ended the year 6.7% above its 1 July level. Q3 earnings have been strong, and futures turned positive after the initial dip.
tension_points.bear_case: Elevated yields limit multiple expansion, tech is exposed to AI regulation headlines and Iran, and consensus earnings leave little room for disappointment. The balance of risks for US equities is tilted to the downside with some volatility expected.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A resumption of military action against Iran that triggers an oil-driven inflation shock and a more hawkish Fed.

tension_points.bull_case: Deteriorating growth, weak real income and falling savings could revive safe-haven demand for long-dated Treasuries, favoring the long end over the front end.
tension_points.bear_case: Renewed Iran escalation would cause a bear flattening as the front end reprices inflation and Fed tightening, while fiscal deficits and political division push the term premium higher.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A meaningful equity correction that shifts focus from inflation to recession risk would favor long-dated Treasuries.
